1.title: Tool Implementation
1.text: Welcome to Module eleven: Tool Implementation. This module covers the skills tool implementation. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. Tool use and function calling: the round trip from definition to result. Writing tool descriptions and schemas. Error handling in tools. Patterns: harness dispatch, client-side versus server-side tools, approval patterns. Tool set construction best practices.

1.title: Case Check-In: Tidewater Connects the Policy System
1.text: Our running case is Tidewater Insurance. Tidewater Connects the Policy System. The assistant must look up policies, check claim status and open a payment request. These actions live in Tidewater's internal systems: Claude cannot reach them on its own.

1.title: The Tool Round Trip
1.text: The Tool Round Trip. The figure shows this: The tool round trip: definitions go in, Claude returns tool use, your code runs the function, the tool result goes back, Claude answers.

1.title: The Tool Round Trip, continued
1.text: The Tool Round Trip, continued. Define. Each tool has a name, a description and an input schema (Jason Schema). Call. Claude decides to use a tool and returns a tool use block (name, id, input); stop reason is "tool use". Run. Your harness validates the input and runs the function (this is the dispatch: map tool name to code). Return. Send a tool result (matching tool use id) in the next user message. Continue. Claude reads the result and answers or calls another tool; stop on end turn.

1.title: The Tool Round Trip, continued
1.text: The Tool Round Trip, continued. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: The Tool Round Trip, continued
1.text: The Tool Round Trip, continued. Claude can request several tools at once (parallel tool calls); return all results together. tool choice controls whether a tool must be called (auto, any, a named tool, none). Descriptions drive selection: say what the tool does, its inputs, when to use it and when not to; precise schemas (patterns, enums) prevent bad input. Forced tool use (tool choice of any or a named tool) is not supported on some current models; see the define-tools page for alternatives such as strict tool use. As of eight November two thousand twenty-six. Exam tip: The model's tool arguments are untrusted input: validate them in your harness before running anything.

1.title: Client-Side Versus Server-Side Tools
1.text: Client-Side Versus Server-Side Tools. The figure shows this: Where the code runs: client tools run in your application; server tools run on Anthropic's infrastructure.

1.title: Client-Side Versus Server-Side Tools, continued
1.text: Client-Side Versus Server-Side Tools, continued. Runs. Client tools: In your application. Server tools: On Anthropic's infrastructure. Examples. Client tools: Your internal A P I s (application programming interface); bash and text editor (Anthropic-defined schemas, your execution). Server tools: web search, web fetch, code execution, tool search. Flow. Client tools: tool use to you run it to tool result. Server tools: You see results directly; no execution on your side. Control. Client tools: Full: validation, permissions, logging. Server tools: Less: configure and trust the platform. Use for. Client tools: Internal systems, private data, side effects. Server tools: General capabilities that need no access to your systems. Exam tip: Internal systems and private data call for client tools; server tools suit general capabilities such as web search.

1.title: Error Handling, Dispatch and Approval
1.text: Error Handling, Dispatch and Approval. Return errors to the model in the tool result with is error: true and a clear message (what failed, whether to retry, what to try instead). An exception that crashes the harness gives the model nothing to recover from. Validate input before running (types, ranges, authorization of the caller, not just the model's request). The model's arguments are untrusted input. Timeouts and idempotency: bound tool runtime; give side-effecting tools an idempotency key so retries are safe. Prune results: return only the fields needed (Module nine).

1.title: Approval patterns
1.text: Approval patterns. Auto-approve. Read-only, low-risk tools. Human confirmation. Sensitive or irreversible actions (payments, deletions, emails). Policy or permission rules and hooks. Deterministic allow, deny or ask by tool and arguments. Dry run then commit. Show what would change; apply after approval.

1.title: Approval patterns, continued
1.text: Approval patterns, continued. The figure shows this: A safe tool call path: validate, check policy, ask a human when needed, execute, prune the result, return structured errors.

1.title: Building a Good Tool Set
1.text: Building a Good Tool Set. Few, distinct tools. Too many or overlapping tools degrade selection. Clear names and boundary-stating descriptions. The description is the main selection signal. One purpose per tool with a precise schema. Reliable use and testing. Consistent naming and error format. Predictable behavior. Return concise, relevant results. Saves context. Least privilege. A tool exposes only what it needs; separate read and write tools. Test tool selection with ambiguous requests. Catches misrouting early. Exam tip: Wrong tool chosen or misused to improve the description and schema first; sensitive action to approval gate plus validation in code, not a prompt sentence.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Definition: name, description, input schema. Round trip: tool use (stop reason: tool use) to run to tool result (same id) to continue until end turn. Dispatch: Harness maps tool name to code; validate input; model arguments are untrusted. Client versus server: Client tools run in your app (internal systems). Errors: tool result with is error: true and a useful message; timeouts; idempotency. Approval: Auto for read-only; human confirmation or hooks for sensitive actions. Tool set: Few, distinct, well described, least privilege, concise results.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. Claude must call Tidewater's internal claims A P I. Where does the A P I call actually run? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. For client tools the application executes the function and returns a tool result.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. Which is a server tool? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Server tools such as web search and code execution run on Anthropic's infrastructure.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. A tool call arrives with stop reason: "tool use". What must the application do next? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. The loop continues by returning the result for the specific call.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. A tool fails with a timeout. What should the harness return to Claude? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Structured errors let the model recover; crashes and fake successes hide the failure.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. Claude keeps choosing get customer when the user asks about a policy, because both descriptions are three words long. What is the best first step? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Descriptions are the primary selection signal; improve them before adding infrastructure.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. A tool initiates payments. Which control is most appropriate? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Sensitive actions need enforced approval and safe retry behavior.

1.title: Practice Question 7
1.text: Question seven. Select two. Which two describe good tool set design? The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and E. Distinct, well described tools and concise results improve selection and keep context small.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all seven answers. Question one: D. Question two: D. Question three: D. Question four: C. Question five: A. Question six: A. Question seven: B and E. In the next module, we continue the course.
